items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: In 2007, rather than excavate the Nanhai One where it lay off southern China, archaeologists lifted the whole merchant ship without first unloading its ______ in a steel caisson along with tons of surrounding sediment, the ship was transported to a purpose-built museum, where its contents were carefully excavated.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “without first unloading its cargo.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Encased in a steel caisson along with tons of surrounding sediment,” which describes its subject, “the ship,” and then gives the main verb “was transported.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma attaches the participial phrase to the first clause, so the main clause “the ship was transported to a purpose-built museum ...” is joined to the first independent clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: “Which was encased” makes the phrase a description of the cargo inside the first sentence, so the clause “the ship was transported ...” still follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “encased in a steel caisson” reads as a description of the cargo, but the comma after “sediment” then joins two independent clauses, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology). Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): opener of 11 words, a past participle that can describe clause 1's last noun (“cargo encased in a steel caisson” reads naturally in A, B and C); the splice shows only at “the ship was transported,” 11 words after the blank, so the cue is outside a 6-word window; the run is the whole 49-word passage (one sentence); reasoning steps 3. No logic-wrong distractor (the template's band-7 models have none). Menu differs from w1b1_01 (which used and / none / comma / period).
band7_moves: opener of 11 words, a past participle that could modify clause 1's last noun
glued and which-clause options read as natural descriptions of the cargo until the splice 11 words later
one-sentence run of 49 words

fixes: why_wrong B quoted “which was enclosed”; the option says “which was encased”

band7.why: S1_period on the 3.28 and 3.10 shape: an 11-word past-participle opener that reads naturally on clause 1’s last noun (cargo), so the comma, which-was and glued options hold until the splice at “the ship was transported,” 11 words after the blank; one 49-word run.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a noun-phrase appositive opener
items.passage: To get its spores eaten by herbivores, which avoid grass surrounding their droppings, the dung-dwelling fungus Pilobolus relies on a pressurized ______ swollen, fluid-filled stalk capped by a capsule of spores, this structure ruptures when mature, propelling the capsule as far as two meters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a pressurized launcher.” The second sentence opens with the noun phrase “A swollen, fluid-filled stalk capped by a capsule of spores,” which describes its subject, “this structure,” and then gives the verb “ruptures.” A period is needed between the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes the noun phrase a description of “launcher,” so the clause “this structure ruptures ...” is joined to the first independent clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “Which is a ...” attaches the description to “launcher” within the first sentence, and the clause “this structure ruptures ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “That is a ...” also makes the description part of the first sentence, so the comma before “this structure” joins two independent clauses, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (mycology). Band-7 checks: the opener is a 10-word noun-phrase appositive that renames clause 1's last noun (the 3.8 and 940ff6f7 move), so A, C and D read as an ordinary appositive or relative clause until “this structure,” 11 words after the blank; the run is the whole 44-word passage; reasoning steps 3. Two added-word variants as in 4b424102 (“who are known” / “, who are known”).
band7_moves: opener is a 10-word noun phrase that renames clause 1's last noun and could hang on it
two added-word distractors (which is a / that is a) that read as natural until the second subject
splice cue 11 words after the blank

fixes: trimmed passage from 48 to 44 words (models’ median 44); the 10-word opener and the 11-word cue distance kept

band7.why: The 3.8 move with its menu: a 10-word noun-phrase opener that renames and could hang on “launcher,” so the comma, which-is and that-is options read as normal until “this structure,” 11 words after the blank.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before an infinitive opener
items.passage: The deep waters of Lake Kivu, along Rwanda’s western border, hold huge quantities of dissolved ______ exploit this resource, a Rwandan power project extracts gas-laden water from the depths and pipes the separated methane ashore, where it is burned to generate electricity.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “dissolved methane.” The second sentence opens with the infinitive phrase “To exploit this resource,” which gives the purpose of the action that follows, and its main clause is “a Rwandan power project extracts gas-laden water from the depths ...” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma attaches “to exploit this resource” to the first clause, so the main clause “a Rwandan power project extracts ...” is joined to the first independent clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “In order to” says the waters hold methane for the purpose of exploiting it, which is illogical, and the clause “a Rwandan power project extracts ...” still follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, “to exploit this resource” runs into the first clause, and the comma after “resource” then joins two independent clauses, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (limnology and energy). Band 6 by plan: short purpose opener (4 words) in the manner of 5ee7fb04's infinitive; no semicolon option, since “; to exploit this resource, a Rwandan power project extracts ...” would be a second correct answer.

band7.why: A 4-word infinitive opener right after the blank keeps the cue inside a 6-word window (5ee7fb04 shape); planned band 6.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1 (contrast with the previous sentence), semicolon after it
items.passage: The Sogdians of Central Asia are remembered principally as merchants who dominated commerce along the Silk Road. The early fourth-century Sogdian documents known as the Ancient Letters are not exclusively ______ one is an indignant message from a woman named Miwnay, whose husband had abandoned her in a Chinese frontier town.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The previous sentence says the Sogdians are remembered principally as merchants, and the clause “the Ancient Letters are not exclusively commercial, however” runs against that impression, so “however” belongs at the end of this clause, set off by a comma. The semicolon after “however” then joins this clause to the next one, “one is an indignant message ...,” which gives an example of a letter that is not commercial.

A.why_wrong: The semicolon before “however” makes the adverb open the second clause, illogically presenting Miwnay’s message as contrary to the claim that the letters are not exclusively commercial; the message is an example of that claim.

B.why_wrong: Commas alone can't join the two independent clauses; the comma after “however” creates a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation after “commercial,” the two independent clauses run together, and “however” is attached to the second clause, where it would illogically signal a contrast with the first.

items.notes: Subject: history (Silk Road documents). Band-7 checks: the adverb closes clause 1, which qualifies the previous sentence (merchants, so the letters should be commercial); clause 2 is an example of clause 1, so A's contrast fails on meaning, the cue sitting in the previous sentence; B and D fail on rule. Run 35 words.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which corrects the impression left by the previous sentence
logic-wrong distractor (; however,) is the taught pattern and fails only against the previous sentence
clause 2 is an example of clause 1, so no contrast reading survives

review.attribution: Miwnay’s letter among the Sogdian Ancient Letters reads right from recall; kept, not searched

band7.why: The b771d175 and be37d4ae move: “however” closes a clause that corrects the previous sentence, the taught “; however,” fails only on meaning against sentence 1, and clause 2 is an example of clause 1, so no contrast reading survives.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, period before the next sentence
items.passage: The Chinese philosopher Mozi, who taught in the fifth century BCE, denounced wars of conquest as theft and murder committed on a huge scale. He did not oppose all warfare, ______ and his disciples became specialists in defending walled cities, traveling to assist smaller states threatened by invasion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma before the blank sets off “however,” which ends the clause “He did not oppose all warfare, however” and contrasts it with Mozi’s denunciation of conquest in the previous sentence. The words that follow, “He and his disciples became specialists ...,” form a new independent clause, so a period is needed after “however.”

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation after “however,” the two independent clauses run together.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join the independent clause ending in “however” to the independent clause “he and his disciples became specialists ...,” so this is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “But” needs a comma before it to join two independent clauses, and it would also present the disciples’ skill at defending cities as contrary to Mozi’s not opposing all warfare, which is illogical.

items.notes: Subject: philosophy (early Chinese thought). Band 6 by plan, on 2bb7416a's frame (adverb already set off by a comma in the passage, the boundary after it). No semicolon option (it would be a twin of the period key), and no “, and” or “, so” option, which would be acceptable after the parenthetical “however.”

review.attribution: Mozi’s condemnation of conquest and his school’s defensive expertise read right from recall; kept

band7.why: The 2bb7416a (3.7) frame and menu: the adverb is already set off in the passage, and the splice, fused and but options fail on rule at the blank; planned band 6.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a single specified item (noun phrase with a relative clause)
items.passage: Fante Asafo companies, traditional warrior associations in the coastal towns of present-day Ghana, fly appliquéd cloth flags whose images illustrate proverbs and taunt rival companies. Before 1957, most of these flags shared one borrowed ______ British Union Jack, which filled the corner nearest the pole until Ghana’s independence, when the new national flag took its place.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “Before 1957, most of these flags shared one borrowed emblem” is complete and announces an item that the rest of the sentence names. A colon correctly introduces that item, the noun phrase “the British Union Jack, which filled the corner nearest the pole until Ghana’s independence ...”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “the British Union Jack, which filled ...” is a noun phrase followed by a relative clause, not an independent clause.

C.why_wrong: “It was” turns what follows into an independent clause, so the comma joins two independent clauses, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “The British Union Jack, which filled the corner ... took its place” as a fragment: “filled” and “took” are the verbs of the relative clause and the when-clause, so there is no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts (textiles, Ghana). Band-7 checks: the specified item is a noun phrase whose relative clause and when-clause carry finite verbs (“filled,” “took”), so the period and semicolon options look like they introduce a sentence; menu as e9aee0d8 (colon / semicolon / comma + it was / period) but the announcing phrase is a counted noun (“one borrowed emblem”), not e9aee0d8's comparative.
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon contains finite verbs in a relative clause and a when-clause
period and semicolon options read as introducing a full sentence
comma + added it was option (splice)

band7.why: The e9aee0d8 menu and move: a complete clause announcing “one borrowed emblem,” then a noun phrase whose relative clause and when-clause carry finite verbs, so the period and semicolon options look like they start a sentence.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a single specified item
items.passage: The Madaba Map, a sixth-century floor mosaic in a Jordanian church, depicts the territory between Lebanon and the Nile Delta, identifying settlements, rivers, and roads. Its creators devoted their most elaborate detail to one city in ______ Jerusalem, whose walls, gates, and colonnaded main street are clearly visible.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “Its creators devoted their most elaborate detail to one city in particular” is complete and announces a specific city. A colon correctly introduces that city, “Jerusalem,” together with the description that follows it.

A.why_wrong: “Jerusalem, whose walls ... are clearly visible” is a noun phrase with a relative clause, not an independent clause, so a semicolon can't introduce it.

B.why_wrong: Without punctuation, the name “Jerusalem” runs straight into the phrase “in particular,” and nothing marks it as the city the clause announces.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “Jerusalem, whose walls ... are clearly visible” as a fragment; “are” is the verb of the relative clause, not of a main clause.

items.notes: Subject: history (Byzantine cartography). Band 6: the 3.22 menu (period, semicolon, none, colon). No comma or lone-dash option: either mark before “Jerusalem” could be defended.

band7.why: The 3.22 menu with a short announcing phrase and a single name after the blank; the cue is local; planned band 6.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive: title and name as the subject of a clause
items.passage: Javanese artist Raden Saleh’s 1857 painting The Arrest of Pangeran Diponegoro shows the captured prince as defiant. Decades earlier, Dutch ______ had portrayed the same scene with the prince appearing resigned to his captivity, a depiction that Saleh’s painting pointedly rejects.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Dutch painter” is a title that identifies Nicolaas Pieneman, and together they are the subject of the clause “Dutch painter Nicolaas Pieneman had portrayed the same scene.” Because the name is essential to identifying the painter, no punctuation should separate “painter” from “Nicolaas Pieneman,” and no comma should separate the subject from its verb, “had portrayed.”

A.why_wrong: Setting “Nicolaas Pieneman” off with commas treats the name as extra information, but without it “Dutch painter” does not tell the reader who completed the earlier version.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “Pieneman” separates the subject of the clause from its verb, “had portrayed.”

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “Dutch painter” from the name it identifies, “Nicolaas Pieneman.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (painting, Indonesia). Band 6 on 3.14's option shape (both slots varied); the title and name open their clause after the short phrase “Decades earlier,” with no determiner before them (the 3.14 and 4dcedc31 shape), so the comma pair in A cannot be defended as a nonrestrictive appositive; the name is followed directly by its verb, so no comma after it can be defended either.

fixes: trimmed passage from 45 to 41 words (models’ median 41); explanation and why_wrong C updated to “had portrayed”
review.attribution: Raden Saleh’s 1857 painting answering Nicolaas Pieneman’s earlier submission scene reads right from recall; kept

band7.why: Title plus name followed directly by the verb, with no later material tempting a comma (4dcedc31 shape); planned band 6.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus and, second clause opening with a because-clause
items.passage: At Mehrgarh, a Neolithic settlement in present-day Pakistan, archaeologists discovered eleven molars with holes drilled into their ______ because the edges of several holes were worn smooth, researchers concluded that the procedure was performed on living patients, who kept chewing with those teeth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text joins two independent clauses: “archaeologists discovered eleven molars with holes drilled into their crowns” and “researchers concluded that the procedure was performed on living patients,” which opens with the introductory clause “because the edges of several holes were worn smooth.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins the two.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the because-clause attaches to the first clause, and the comma after “smooth” then joins two independent clauses, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology, early dentistry). Plan asked band 7, but S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items (band7/boundaries.md, appendix), so it is written as a strong band 6: the second clause opens with a because-clause, so the bare-comma and no-mark options look like a dependent clause attaching normally (B also reads as a causal clause of clause 1 until the second subject).

fixes: trimmed passage from 48 to 43 words (models’ median 43); explanation quotes updated

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6: the because-clause opening clause 2 makes the bare-comma and no-mark options read as ordinary subordination until “researchers,” 10 words on.

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around a supplement that itself contains parentheses
items.passage: The archives left by Assyrian merchants at Kanesh, a commercial outpost in central Anatolia, around 1900 BCE—some 23,000 clay tablets, many of them letters from relatives in Assur (frequently wives and sisters who made the textiles the merchants ______ offer an unusually intimate perspective on ancient long-distance trade.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “1900 BCE” opens a supplementary element describing the archives, and inside it a parenthesis opens before “frequently wives and sisters.” The closing parenthesis after “sold” ends the inner element, and a closing dash is then needed to end the outer one before the verb “offer.”

A.why_wrong: This closes the parentheses but not the dash, leaving the element that opens after “1900 BCE” unclosed when the main verb “offer” arrives.

B.why_wrong: This closes the dash element but leaves the parenthesis that begins “(frequently wives and sisters” without its closing mark.

D.why_wrong: A comma can't close an element that opens with a dash; the marks on either side of the element must match.

items.notes: Subject: history (Old Assyrian trade). Band-7 checks: two levels of supplement in one option (the 83898524 move: a parenthesis inside a dash element); the opening dash is 22 words before the blank and the opening parenthesis 10, so both partners sit outside a 6-word window; the run is the whole 48-word sentence. Menu differs from 83898524's (no comma inside the parenthesis).
band7_moves: parentheses nested inside a dash pair, both closed at the blank
partners 10 and 22 words before the blank
each wrong option closes only one level or the wrong mark

band7.why: The 83898524 move: a parenthesis nested inside a dash element, both closed at the blank, with the dash partner 22 words back and the parenthesis 10; each wrong option closes only one level or mismatches the pair.

items.subtype: Colon between independent clauses: the second explains the first
items.passage: In the dry scrublands of eastern Kenya, dwarf mongooses often forage alongside several species of hornbill. The partnership benefits both ______ the birds snap up insects that the mongooses scare out of the grass, and the mongooses heed the hornbills’ alarm calls when hawks approach.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “The partnership benefits both animals” makes a general claim, and the clause that follows explains it by describing what each animal gains. A colon is used to join two independent clauses when the second explains the first.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, “and” can't join these two long independent clauses, and “and” would present the explanation as one more fact rather than as the reason both animals benefit.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: science (animal behavior, mutualism). Band 6 as planned; 8772475b's menu (and / comma / none / colon). No “while” option: “, while the birds snap up insects” could be read as acceptable.

band7.why: The 8772475b menu without its band-7 relation-word trap (“while” left out because it could be defended), so the and/comma/none options fail on rule; planned band 6.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: Marketing researchers Joseph Nunes and Xavier Drèze distributed loyalty cards to car wash customers, each card requiring eight purchases to earn a free wash. Customers whose cards contained ten spaces but came with two already ______ were nearly twice as likely as the others to complete their cards.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the long noun phrase “Customers whose cards contained ten spaces but came with two already stamped,” and its verb is “were.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject “Customers whose cards ... stamped” from its verb, “were.”

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow an independent clause, but “Customers whose cards ... stamped” is only the subject of the sentence.

D.why_wrong: A single dash between the subject and the verb has no partner and no role; it splits the subject from “were.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (consumer behavior, the endowed progress effect, 2006). Plan asked band 7, but S4_subj_verb has no band-7 official items, so it is written as a strong band 6: a 12-word subject ending in a participle (“already stamped”) where a pause, and so a comma, feels natural.

review.attribution: Nunes and Drèze’s car wash loyalty-card study (8 stamps vs 10 with 2 pre-stamped) reads right from recall; kept

band7.why: S4_subj_verb has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 with a 12-word subject ending in a participle (“already stamped”) where a pause feels natural.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus and, second clause opening with an adverb
items.passage: In 1653, Neapolitan banker Lorenzo de Tonti proposed an unusual scheme for financing the French government. Under his plan, investors would buy shares in a fund paying yearly interest, with each deceased investor’s share redistributed among the remaining ______ eventually a single survivor would collect all the interest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence joins two independent clauses: “investors would buy shares in a fund paying yearly interest, with each deceased investor’s share redistributed among the remaining investors” and “eventually a single survivor would collect all the interest.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; “eventually” opens the second clause rather than linking the two.

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history, the tontine). The second clause opens with the adverb “eventually,” so the bare comma looks like it sets off an adverb, as medium items place a short opener after the boundary.

fixes: trimmed passage from 53 to 48 words (models’ median 49.5); explanation quotes updated
review.attribution: Lorenzo de Tonti’s 1653 tontine proposal reads right from recall; kept

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before an although-clause opener
items.passage: In the seventeenth century, Ottoman writer Evliya Çelebi spent some forty years journeying from the Balkans to Egypt, recording his observations in a ten-volume work called the Seyahatname, or Book of ______ some of his stories strain belief, historians prize the work for its detailed accounts of cities, crafts, and languages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with the work’s English title, “Book of Travels.” The second sentence opens with the dependent clause “Although some of his stories strain belief,” followed by its main clause, “historians prize the work ...” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma attaches the although-clause to the first sentence, so the main clause “historians prize the work ...” is joined to it with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, the although-clause runs into the first sentence, and the comma after “belief” then joins two independent clauses, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” without a comma can't join these two long independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: literature (travel writing, Ottoman). Medium: a short dependent-clause opener (7 words) after the boundary. No semicolon option: “; although some of his stories strain belief, historians prize ...” would be correct.

items.subtype: Closing a comma pair around a participial phrase between subject and verb
items.passage: In the Scottish Hebrides, newly woven tweed was traditionally thickened by women who rhythmically pounded the damp cloth against a table. Their waulking songs, performed in Gaelic with a soloist leading and the others responding in ______ helped them keep a steady beat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “songs” opens a supplementary phrase, “performed in Gaelic with a soloist leading and the others responding in chorus,” that describes the songs. A second comma is needed after “chorus” to close the phrase before the verb “helped.”

A.why_wrong: A dash can't close an element that opens with a comma; the marks on either side of the phrase must match.

B.why_wrong: The semicolon separates the subject “Their waulking songs” from its verb, “helped,” and neither side is an independent clause.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma after “chorus,” the supplementary phrase opened by the comma after “songs” is never closed.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music and craft, Scotland). Partner comma 12 words before the blank.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Sheep on North Ronaldsay, the northernmost of Scotland’s Orkney Islands, seldom eat grass. A stone wall built in 1832 to protect the island’s agricultural land runs around almost the entire ______ the animals to the rocky shoreline, where they survive almost exclusively on seaweed for most of the year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “A stone wall built in 1832 to protect the island’s agricultural land runs around almost the entire coast” is followed by the participial phrase “confining the animals to the rocky shoreline,” which describes what the wall does. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this trailing supplementary phrase.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “confining the animals ... for most of the year” has no subject or main verb.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves “Confining the animals to the rocky shoreline, where they survive ... for most of the year” as a fragment with no main clause.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “confining the animals” attaches to “coast,” as if the coast rather than the wall kept the sheep on the shoreline; a comma is needed to separate the main clause from the supplementary phrase.

items.notes: Subject: science (animal husbandry and ecology, Orkney). Menu as 2.4 and 2.26 (semicolon, comma, period, none).

fixes: trimmed passage from 54 to 49 words (models’ median 50); explanation quote updated

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before an explanation (noun phrase)
items.passage: A lightning strike lasts only a fraction of a second, but when it hits sand, the electricity can heat the grains far beyond their melting temperature. The discharge may then leave a permanent record of its ______ fulgurite, a hollow, branching tube of glass that formed as the sand melted and fused.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “The discharge may then leave a permanent record of its path” is complete, and the noun phrase that follows, “a fulgurite, a hollow, branching tube of glass ...,” names that record. A colon correctly introduces this explanation.

band7_moves: trailing absolute phrase whose noun carries a relative clause with a finite verb
semicolon and period options look like they start a clause
the deciding check (no main verb) sits 10+ words after the blank

band7.why: 3.24 (62120607) menu exactly; the absolute phrase’s noun has a relative clause with a finite verb (“that separate”), so semicolon and period look as if a clause follows.

items.subtype: No punctuation between two coordinated that-clauses
items.passage: Biologist Andrew Thurber’s team found that the bristly claws of Kiwa puravida, a crab inhabiting deep-sea methane seeps off Costa Rica, harbor dense populations of ______ and that the crab’s rhythmic claw waving may supply these microorganisms, which it consumes, with oxygen and sulfide.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The verb “found” has two objects, joined by “and”: “that the bristly claws ... harbor dense populations of bacteria” and “that the crab’s rhythmic claw waving may supply these microorganisms ... with oxygen and sulfide.” Because there are only two coordinated elements, no punctuation is needed before “and.”

A.why_wrong: No comma is needed between two coordinated that-clauses; the comma wrongly separates the two objects of “found.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate the two that-clauses, neither of which is an independent clause.

D.why_wrong: A colon can't be used here; “and that the crab’s ...” is the second object of “found,” not an explanation of the first.

items.notes: Subject: science (deep-sea biology, Thurber and colleagues 2011, from recall). Plan asked band 7, but S4_compound has no band-7 official items (band7/boundaries.md, appendix), so it is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6: the first that-clause is long and holds a comma-set appositive, so a balancing comma before “and that” looks natural (3.3's move with that-clauses; 2.23's “and the fact that”).

review.note: Comma before “and that” (A) kept as a wrong option: it neither separates independent clauses nor prevents a misreading, so its only defence is a style preference for long coordinates; College Board keys the same comma wrong in 6ea8c23f (3.3, “regions,”) and states that two coordinates take no punctuation. Thurber: Kiwa puravida bacterial farming by claw waving is his team’s published finding; kept.

band7.why: S4_compound has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on 3.3 (6ea8c23f): the long first that-clause with its appositive pair makes the comma before “and that” tempting.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: When philosopher Antanas Mockus became mayor of Bogotá, Colombia, in 1995, he tried unusual strategies to tame the city’s chaotic traffic. He hired mime artists to silently mock drivers and pedestrians who disregarded traffic ______ over the next decade, the city’s yearly traffic fatalities fell by about half.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “He hired mime artists to silently mock drivers and pedestrians who disregarded traffic rules” and “over the next decade, the city’s yearly traffic fatalities fell by about half” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban policy, Bogotá). Medium: the second clause opens with the short time phrase “over the next decade,” so the bare comma looks like it sets off a phrase (2.5's move). Standard menu (2.2, 2.5).

review.note: Mockus: mime artists in Bogotá traffic are his standard record; kept.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a short prepositional phrase
items.passage: When threatened, the hairy frog of Central Africa can force sharp bones in its hind toes to pierce through its own skin, creating makeshift ______ the claws of other vertebrates, these bony projections lack a protective covering of keratin, the tough protein that forms hair and nails.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “When threatened, the hairy frog ... can force sharp bones ... to pierce through its own skin, creating makeshift claws” is a complete sentence. “Unlike the claws of other vertebrates” describes “these bony projections,” the subject of the next sentence, so a period after “claws” is needed.

B.why_wrong: The comma makes “unlike the claws of other vertebrates” look like part of the first sentence, but “these bony projections lack ...” is a second independent clause, so the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together, and “claws unlike the claws of other vertebrates” garbles the first one.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, “and” can't be used to join these two independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: science (amphibian anatomy). Medium: a 5-word opener before clause 2's subject (2.7's “According to some historians,” and 2.27's “Prior to VisiCalc's release,”). No semicolon option. Facts as reported in 2008 (claws that pierce the skin and lack a keratin sheath); no researcher named.

items.subtype: Comma closing an appositive opened by a comma
items.passage: Filipino director Kidlat Tahimik made Perfumed Nightmare (1977) on a tiny budget, casting himself as the protagonist. His character, a jeepney driver who adores the American space ______ travels to Paris and grows disillusioned with Western promises of technological progress.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The appositive “a jeepney driver who adores the American space program” renames “His character” and is set off from the rest of the sentence. It opens with a comma after “character,” so it must close with a comma after “program” before the verb “travels.”

A.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the appositive opened by the comma after “character” is left unclosed.

C.why_wrong: A dash can't close an appositive that was opened with a comma.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate the subject “His character” from its verb “travels.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Philippine cinema). Partner comma 11 words before the blank. Architecture differs from w1b3_15 (an appositive on the protagonist, not a title after “first feature”).

review.note: Tahimik: Perfumed Nightmare plot as made; kept.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Malian writer Amadou Hampâté Bâ devoted decades to recording the oral histories and epics of the Fulani and Bambara peoples. Addressing UNESCO in 1960, he compared the death of an elder to the burning of a ______ the organization to help preserve such traditions before they disappeared.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Addressing UNESCO in 1960, he compared the death of an elder to the burning of a library” is a complete main clause. “Urging the organization to help preserve such traditions ...” is a participial phrase that describes what Bâ was doing as he spoke, so a comma correctly separates it from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join the main clause to “urging the organization ...,” which is a phrase, not an independent clause.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “Urging the organization to help preserve such traditions before they disappeared” as a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “a library urging the organization” wrongly makes the library the one doing the urging; a comma must separate the main clause from the participial phrase.

items.notes: Subject: literature (West African oral tradition). Medium on 2.4 and 2.26 (trailing -ing phrase). Bâ's 1960 UNESCO remark is reported indirectly rather than quoted, since its English wording varies.

review.note: Hampâté Bâ: the library remark at UNESCO in 1960 is his standard record; kept.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject (ending in a relative clause) and its verb
items.passage: In 2019, biologist Sidney Tamm reported that, unlike the permanent anus of most animals with a complete digestive tract, the opening through which the comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi expels undigested ______ appears only when the animal is about to excrete waste and then disappears until it is needed again.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the that-clause is “the opening through which the comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi expels undigested food,” and its verb is “appears.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.

A.why_wrong: A comma can't separate the subject “the opening ... undigested food” from its verb “appears.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate a subject from its verb.

C.why_wrong: A colon can't separate a subject from its verb.

items.notes: Subject: science (invertebrate anatomy; Sidney Tamm's 2019 report on the comb jelly's transient anus, from recall). Medium: a 12-word subject whose relative clause ends at the blank, after a comma-set “unlike” phrase, so a comma feels natural (2.11's move).

review.note: Tamm: 2019 report of the comb jelly’s transient anus is his published finding; kept.

items.subtype: No punctuation between the two parts of a both ... and compound
items.passage: Nigerian photographer J.D. ’Okhai Ojeikere’s Hairstyles series, begun in 1968 and later numbering nearly 1,000 photographs, documents both the elaborate braided and threaded styles that women wore to weddings and other ______ and the simpler ones that they wore to work each day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Both ... and” joins two noun phrases that serve as objects of “documents”: “the elaborate braided and threaded styles that women wore to weddings and other celebrations” and “the simpler ones that they wore to work each day.” With only two coordinated elements, no punctuation belongs before “and.”

B.why_wrong: No comma is needed between the two parts of the compound joined by “both ... and.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate two noun phrases that together form the object of “documents.”

D.why_wrong: A colon can't separate the two parts of a compound object; “and the simpler ones ...” does not explain what comes before it.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Nigerian photography). Medium S4_compound (2.23): the first conjunct is long and holds its own “and,” so a comma before the second “and” looks natural. Name written “J.D.” as the photographer is usually credited.

review.note: Ojeikere: Hairstyles series from 1968, nearly 1,000 photographs; kept.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: In the Peruvian Amazon, the Shanay-Timpishka River reaches temperatures high enough to kill small animals that fall in. Although the nearest active volcano is hundreds of kilometers away, the river is heated ______ groundwater rising along deep fractures in Earth’s crust.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “the river is heated by groundwater rising along deep fractures in Earth’s crust,” “groundwater” is the object of the preposition “by.” No punctuation should come between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon can't separate the preposition “by” from its object.

B.why_wrong: A comma can't separate the preposition “by” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash can't separate the preposition “by” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: science (geology and hydrology, Peruvian Amazon). Preposition not yet used by our S4_object items.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Every year at the end of the rainy season, Wodaabe herders in Niger and Chad gather for the Gerewol, a weeklong celebration. Young men decorate their faces with pigments, adorn themselves with beaded ornaments, and perform elaborate dances while young women watch and ______ the dancers they consider most attractive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “young women watch and choose the dancers they consider most attractive,” “the dancers” is the object of the verb “choose.” No punctuation should come between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon can't separate the verb “choose” from its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma can't separate the verb “choose” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash can't separate the verb “choose” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: social science (anthropology, Sahel pastoralists).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Desert locusts usually avoid one another, but crowding can make them swarm. In 2009, researchers linked this transformation to the chemical ______ solitary locusts injected with it began to act like swarming ones.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2009, researchers linked this transformation to the chemical serotonin” and “solitary locusts injected with it began to act like swarming ones” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

D.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “and” here; nothing is set off between “and” and the subject “solitary locusts.”

items.notes: Subject: science (insect behavior and neurochemistry; the 2009 serotonin finding, researchers unnamed). No bare “serotonin and” option: with clauses this short, a comma-less “and” could be defended (b1 note on w2b1_21).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Venezuelan artist Carlos Cruz-Diez treated color as an experience rather than a permanent property of objects. Because the narrow stripes in his Physichromie series appear to shift in color as spectators walk past ______ the works never look identical twice.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Because the narrow stripes ... appear to shift in color as spectators walk past them” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause “the works never look identical twice.” A comma after “them” correctly separates the introductory clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A comma is needed to mark the end of the introductory dependent clause before the main clause begins.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join a dependent clause to a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves the dependent clause beginning “Because” as a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Latin American kinetic and op art).

review.note: Cruz-Diez: Physichromie series as described; kept.

items.subtype: Direct question after a question word: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: Thousands of massive stone jars, some considerably taller than an adult, are distributed across the Plain of Jars in northern Laos. What ______ Because human remains and burial pits have been discovered nearby, most archaeologists believe the jars served a funerary purpose.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “What” begins a direct question, so the subject and the helping verb are inverted (“were the jars used for”) and the sentence ends with a question mark. The next sentence then answers the question.

A.why_wrong: A direct question beginning with “What” needs inverted word order (“were the jars”), not statement order.

C.why_wrong: Statement order with a period leaves “What the jars were used for” as a fragment rather than a question.

D.why_wrong: The word order is correct for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology, Laos). Direct form (1.18, 1.30), since b1's question item was embedded.

items.subtype: Comma before a sentence-final nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: From about 2500 to 1500 BCE, Kerma, a city on the Nile in present-day Sudan, was the capital of a powerful kingdom. At its center stood a monumental mud-brick temple now known as the Western ______ still rises approximately 18 meters above the surrounding landscape.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “At its center stood a monumental mud-brick temple now known as the Western Deffufa” is a complete main clause. The clause “which still rises approximately 18 meters ...” adds information about a temple already identified by name, so it is nonrestrictive and must be set off with a comma.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join the main clause to the relative clause beginning with “which,” which is not an independent clause.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “Which still rises approximately 18 meters above the surrounding landscape” as a fragment.

D.why_wrong: A relative clause that adds information about a named structure is nonrestrictive and needs a comma before “which.”

items.notes: Subject: history (ancient Sudan). Kept clear of “Nubian” wording used in w1b2_09.

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: Kaurna, the language of the Aboriginal people of South Australia’s Adelaide Plains, had lost its last fluent speakers by the early twentieth ______ since the 1990s, community members and linguists have revived it using vocabularies and a grammar compiled by missionaries in the 1840s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Kaurna ... had lost its last fluent speakers by the early twentieth century” and “since the 1990s, community members and linguists have revived it ...” are both independent clauses. A semicolon correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

items.notes: Subject: language (Aboriginal language revival, South Australia). Menu of 1.4 (comma, none, “and”). No period option.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a long noun-phrase appositive
items.passage: In 2002, researchers exploring California’s Monterey Canyon with a remotely operated vehicle discovered a gray whale skeleton covered in what looked like small red ______ with neither a mouth nor a gut, these animals penetrate the bones with rootlike tissues that house symbiotic bacteria.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2002, researchers ... discovered a gray whale skeleton covered in what looked like small red plumes” is a complete sentence. “Worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” describes “these animals,” the subject of the next sentence (“these animals penetrate the bones ...”), so a period is needed after “plumes.”

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” read as a description of “plumes,” but “these animals penetrate the bones” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together and “plumes worms” garbles the first one.

C.why_wrong: “that were worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” attaches to “plumes,” but “these animals penetrate the bones ...” still follows with only a comma, so the result is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (deep-sea biology, the bone-eating worm Osedax, found on a whale fall in 2002). Band 7: an 8-word noun-phrase opener (0fa289a7, 940ff6f7 shape) that reads as an appositive to “plumes” in A and C; the splice shows only at “these animals,” 9 words past the blank; one 44-word run. Menu of the models (splice, glued, added “that were”); no semicolon option. Researchers unnamed.
band7_moves: opener is an 8-word noun phrase that could rename clause 1's last noun
clause 2's subject arrives 9 words past the blank, outside a 6-word window
added-word option ('that were') keeps a splice

band7.why: S1_period on 0fa289a7: the 8-word noun-phrase opener “Worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” reads as an appositive to “plumes” in A and C, and the splice shows only at “these animals,” 9 words past the blank; 44-word run; splice, glued and added “that were” menu as in 0fa289a7.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a because-clause
items.passage: In 1999, construction workers quarrying gravel in Veracruz, Mexico, unearthed a serpentine slab incised with 62 ______ several of these symbols recur in consistent sequences, much as words do, many specialists regard the slab, now called the Cascajal Block, as the earliest known example of writing in the Americas.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1999, construction workers ... unearthed a serpentine slab incised with 62 signs” is a complete sentence. The next sentence is “Because several of these symbols recur ..., many specialists regard the slab ... as the earliest known example of writing in the Americas”: the because-clause introduces its main clause, “many specialists regard,” so a period goes after “signs.”

A.why_wrong: The comma makes the because-clause seem to explain the first sentence, but “many specialists regard the slab ...” is then a second independent clause joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation the because-clause attaches to the first clause, and “many specialists regard the slab ...” follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “that” would start a relative clause about the signs, but the words after it (“many specialists regard the slab ...”) form a complete clause with nothing missing, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: history (Olmec-era inscribed slab from Veracruz, reported in 2006). Band 7: clause 2 opens with a subordinator (615f001e), so A and C read as a natural because-clause on clause 1 until “many specialists” arrives 13 words past the blank; the because-clause carries its own “much as” interrupter. No semicolon or “and” option (each would make a correct sentence). No researcher named.
band7_moves: clause 2 opens with a subordinate clause, so the comma reads as legal
clause 2's subject arrives 13 words past the blank
added-word 'that,' option as in a872c60a

band7.why: 615f001e move: clause 2 opens with “Because,” so “, because” and “ because” read as a legal subordinate clause on clause 1 until “many specialists regard” arrives 13 words past the blank; 49-word run; added-word “that,” option.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence's subject is a gerund phrase
items.passage: In 1978, faced with a shortage of incubators, doctors at a maternity hospital in Bogotá, Colombia, began asking mothers of premature infants to carry their babies against their bare ______ newborns skin-to-skin in this way stabilized their temperature and encouraged breastfeeding, and the method, called kangaroo mother care, has since spread worldwide.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “to carry their babies against their bare chests.” In the second sentence, the gerund phrase “Holding newborns skin-to-skin in this way” is the subject of “stabilized,” so it must begin a new sentence after a period.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “holding newborns skin-to-skin” look like a phrase describing the mothers, which leaves “stabilized their temperature” without a subject; read as a subject, the phrase starts a second clause joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: “while holding newborns skin-to-skin in this way” attaches to the first clause, so the verb “stabilized” is left with no subject.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “chests holding newborns ...” runs the two sentences together, and “stabilized” has no subject.

items.notes: Subject: science (medicine: kangaroo mother care, begun in Bogotá in 1978). Band 6: gerund-subject opener (73a6603c) with a different menu (while-phrase and glued options instead of “; by adding”); the comma version reads as a participle on the mothers until “stabilized” 6 words past the blank. No semicolon option. Doctors unnamed.

fixes: explanation and why_wrong for A, B and D quoted “kept” / “kept them warm”, which the passage does not contain; now “stabilized” / “stabilized their temperature”

band7.why: Target 6. Gerund-subject opener (73a6603c, band 6); the comma version reads as a participle on the mothers until “stabilized” 7 words past the blank, but a gerund subject is the band-6 opener type, not the band-7 appositive that could rename clause 1’s last noun.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1 (contrast with the previous sentence), semicolon after it
items.passage: The trap-jaw ant Odontomachus bauri, native to Central and South American rainforests, captures prey by releasing its spring-loaded mandibles, which snap shut at velocities of up to 64 meters per second. Those mandibles serve more than a predatory ______ an ant that strikes them against the ground can catapult itself away from potential attackers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence presents the mandibles as a way to capture prey, and “Those mandibles serve more than a predatory function” runs against that, so “however” belongs at the end of this clause, set off by a comma. The semicolon then joins the clause to the next one, “an ant that strikes them against the ground can catapult itself away from potential attackers,” which gives the other use.

B.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the start of the second clause signals a contrast between “serve more than a predatory function” and “an ant ... can catapult itself away from potential attackers,” but the second clause is an example of the first, not a contrast with it.

C.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “however,” the two independent clauses are joined by commas alone.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma before “however” and with only a comma after it, the two independent clauses are still joined by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: science (ant biomechanics; jaw speeds of 35 to 64 meters per second, escape jumps). Band 7: “however” closes clause 1, which corrects the impression left by sentence 1 (mandibles for capturing prey); B, the taught “; however,” placement, fails only on meaning, the cue sitting in the previous sentence. “however” is never offered in a position where it could read as “in whatever way” (D keeps a comma after it), and no “though” option (b2 lesson). No researcher named.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which answers the previous sentence
logic-wrong '; however,' distractor (b771d175, c06af4d8)
clause 2 elaborates clause 1, so no contrast reading of B survives

review.note: “; however,” option (B) judged not defensible, so kept as the band-7 logic trap: clause 2 (the escape jump) is the non-predatory function clause 1 announces, so “however” between them has nothing to contrast; same relation as c06af4d8 and b771d175, whose “; however,” distractors fail the same way. Unlike the b2 “, though” case, “however” here can never read as a subordinator (D keeps a comma after it).

band7.why: c06af4d8 and b771d175 shape: “however” closes clause 1, which corrects the predatory framing of sentence 1; B, the taught “; however,” placement, fails only on meaning with the cue in the previous sentence; C and D are splices. The 26-word run is short of the band-7 range, as in the official adverb items.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, period after it
items.passage: Livonian, a Finnic language once spoken in fishing villages along Latvia’s coast, lost its last native speaker, Grizelda Kristiņa, in 2013. The language hasn’t ______ descendants of Livonian families in Latvia continue to study it, and linguists have compiled dictionaries and grammars to support its revitalization.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The language hasn’t disappeared, however” contrasts with the first sentence’s news that the last native speaker died, so “however” ends that clause, set off by a comma. A period then begins the next sentence, “Many descendants of Livonian families in Latvia continue to study it ...,” which supports the claim that the language survives.

A.why_wrong: “however” at the start of the second clause would signal a contrast between the language not disappearing and descendants studying it, but the second clause supports the first.

B.why_wrong: Commas alone on both sides of “however” join two independent clauses, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no comma before “however,” the adverb runs into the first clause, and the two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: language (Livonian after its last native speaker died in 2013). Band 6: “however. Many” key (2bb7416a shape) with a different menu: one logic-wrong option plus two splices, no fused “however many” (which would read as “no matter how many” and could be grammatical). Details kept general (descendants studying it, dictionaries and grammars).

review.note: “; however,” option (A) judged not defensible: clause 2 (descendants study it, linguists compiled dictionaries to support its revitalization) supports “The language hasn’t disappeared,” so “however” between them has nothing to contrast; same relation as b771d175 (“Compiling isn’t exclusive...; however, any language can incorporate this tool”). No “ however many” option, which could read as “no matter how many.”

band7.why: Target 6. “however. Many” key (2bb7416a, band 6) with one logic-wrong “; however,” option and two splices; the period key is the band-6 adverb shape, not the band-7 clause-1 “, however;” key.

items.subtype: Colon before a specified item, then a period before the next sentence
items.passage: Goffin’s cockatoos feed on the seeds of the sea mango, which are protected by a tough, fibrous husk. To extract them, the birds employ a technique previously documented in the wild in only one other ______ up to three distinct tools from branches, a cockatoo applies them in a particular sequence to reach the seed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “To extract them, the birds employ a technique previously documented in the wild in only one other species” is a complete clause, so a colon can introduce the species it refers to, “the chimpanzee.” A period must then end that sentence, because “Fashioning up to three distinct tools from branches” introduces the subject of a new sentence, “a cockatoo applies them in a particular sequence ....”

items.explanation: “After disease, emigration, and increasing isolation had steadily reduced the population of St Kilda, a remote group of islands far off Scotland’s west coast” is an introductory subordinate clause, and “the last 36 residents asked the British government to evacuate them” begins the main clause. A comma is needed between them; it also closes the description of St Kilda opened by the comma after “Kilda.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs into the main clause, and the description of St Kilda is never closed.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the introductory “After ...” clause is a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: “After disease, emigration, and increasing isolation had steadily reduced the population of St Kilda, ... west coast.” is a dependent clause, so it can’t stand as a sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history (the 1930 evacuation of St Kilda). 1.6 and 1.19 shape: a long introductory After clause, one 41-word sentence.

items.passage: In the early 1800s, Boston merchant Frederic Tudor began shipping ice harvested from New England ponds to customers as far away as India. How ______ Tudor packed the blocks tightly in sawdust, an inexpensive insulating material that dramatically slowed melting.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the ice survived such long journeys?
did the ice survive such long journeys.
the ice survived such long journeys.
did the ice survive such long journeys?
items.explanation: The sentence beginning with “How” is a direct question, so it needs question word order (“did the ice survive”) and a question mark. The next sentence answers it.

A.why_wrong: A direct question needs question word order (“did the ice survive”), not statement order.

B.why_wrong: The word order is right for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark.

C.why_wrong: This is a direct question, so it needs question word order and a question mark, not statement order and a period.

items.notes: Subject: history (Frederic Tudor’s ice trade). 1.18 and 1.30 shape: a direct question opened by How, answered in the next sentence.

items.subtype: Commas between items of a simple series
items.passage: Tuatara, reptiles found only in New Zealand, are the last surviving members of a group that flourished during the age of the dinosaurs. They remain active at temperatures too cold for most ______ grow extremely slowly, and can live for more than a century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things tuatara do: “remain active at temperatures too cold for most reptiles,” “grow extremely slowly,” and “can live for more than a century.” Commas separate the items in a simple series like this one, so a comma is needed after “reptiles,” the end of the first item.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon isn’t used to separate items in a simple series whose items contain no commas.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the first item runs into the second (“too cold for most reptiles grow extremely slowly”), and the sentence no longer makes sense; a comma must separate the items, as one does before “and.”

D.why_wrong: A colon can’t be used to separate items in a series.

items.subtype: Restrictive relative clause with that: no punctuation before it
items.passage: Japan is home to an unusually large number of companies that have operated for centuries. The oldest may have been Kongō Gumi, a ______ built and repaired Buddhist temples from 578 CE until 2006, when financial difficulties led to its absorption by a larger construction company.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That built and repaired Buddhist temples from 578 CE until 2006 ...” is essential to the meaning of “a firm”: it tells what kind of firm Kongō Gumi was. A restrictive clause like this isn’t set off by punctuation, and “that” is needed as the subject of “built and repaired.”

A.why_wrong: Without “that,” nothing serves as the subject of “built and repaired,” so the sentence is ungrammatical.

B.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate “firm” from the restrictive clause that describes it.

D.why_wrong: Without “that,” “a firm built and repaired Buddhist temples” has no subject for “built and repaired.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (business history: Kongō Gumi, the temple builder founded in 578). 1.29 menu (comma, comma + that, that, nothing), with a different frame (“a firm that built and repaired”).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence opens with a noun-phrase appositive that could rename the first sentence's last noun
items.passage: In 1989, a laborer dredging sand in the Philippine province of Laguna discovered a thin copper plate engraved with ______ acknowledgment that a debt had been cleared in 900 CE, the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1989, a laborer dredging sand in the Philippine province of Laguna discovered a thin copper plate engraved with text” is a complete sentence. The noun phrase “An acknowledgment that a debt had been cleared in 900 CE” describes “the inscription,” the subject of the second sentence, so it opens that sentence. A period after “text” marks the boundary between the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “an acknowledgment that a debt had been cleared in 900 CE” seems to rename “text,” but the main clause “the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago” follows, so two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “engraved with text an acknowledgment” runs the first sentence into the noun phrase, and the main clause “the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: Adding “which was” turns the noun phrase into a relative clause about the text, but the main clause “the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago” is still joined to the first sentence by a comma alone, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, found in 1989, dated 900 CE, recording that a debt was cleared; the earliest known written document from the Philippines); real subject, details kept to what is well established, no person named. items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence opens with a prepositional phrase
items.passage: The western underground orchid, found only in a few remnant patches of scrubland in Western Australia, completes its life cycle entirely below ground, even producing its flowers beneath the ______ chlorophyll with which to photosynthesize, the orchid obtains its nutrients from a fungus that is also connected to the roots of neighboring shrubs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The western underground orchid ... completes its life cycle entirely below ground, even producing its flowers beneath the soil” is a complete sentence. The next sentence has its own subject and verb, “the orchid obtains,” and opens with the prepositional phrase “Without chlorophyll with which to photosynthesize.” A period after “soil” separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: With a comma, “without chlorophyll with which to photosynthesize” reads as a tail of the first sentence, but “the orchid obtains its nutrients” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: Adding “and” doesn’t mark the boundary correctly. If “and” joins the two independent clauses, it needs a comma before it; if it links the without-phrase to the first sentence, the clause “the orchid obtains its nutrients” is joined to that sentence by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “beneath the soil without chlorophyll” runs the phrase into the first sentence, and the independent clause “the orchid obtains its nutrients” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: science (Rhizanthella gardneri, the Western Australian orchid that flowers underground and gets nutrients through a fungus shared with shrub roots); real subject, no researcher named. Every wrong option fails on a rule; no semicolon option (twin) and no “, and” option.

band7.why: Band-6 S1_period: 6-word prepositional opener, clause 2's subject 7 words past the blank; two splice disguises plus a fused option, all rule failures.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause: semicolon before “instead,” comma after
items.passage: Fires were so frequent in Edo (present-day Tokyo) that residents called them the “flowers of Edo.” The city’s firefighters, whose hand-operated pumps were too feeble to extinguish major blazes, seldom attempted to put out burning ______ working ahead of the flames, they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The city’s firefighters ... seldom attempted to put out burning buildings” and “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” are both independent clauses, so a semicolon after “buildings” joins them. The adverb “instead” belongs to the second clause, which says what the firefighters did in place of putting out the fires, so the comma after “instead” sets it off from “working ahead of the flames.”

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “working ahead of the flames” runs into the first clause, and the independent clause “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: A comma after “buildings” makes “working ahead of the flames” a tail of the first clause, so the independent clause “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” is joined to the first by commas alone.

C.why_wrong: Commas around “instead” can’t join two independent clauses; the first clause and “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” are still joined by commas alone.

items.notes: Subject: history (firefighting in Edo: weak hand pumps, houses pulled down to stop a fire's spread; the saying that fires were the flowers of Edo); real subject, no person named. Band 6 by plan: a9e5b788 (3.5) menu, two options dropping the adverb, with a 5-word participial phrase after the adverb so clause 2's subject arrives 6 words past the blank. band7.why: a9e5b788 band-6 shape: semicolon plus “instead,” with a 5-word participial phrase before clause 2's subject; every option with the adverb puts a comma after it, so nothing fails on meaning alone.

items.subtype: Adverb closing a dash supplement, then a semicolon joining the clauses (“, respectively;”)
items.passage: In Hindustani classical music, the tabla comprises two drums of contrasting dimensions—a narrow wooden treble drum and a broader metal or clay bass drum, played with the right and left ______ percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “dimensions” opens a supplementary element that names the two drums and says which hand plays each; “respectively” belongs to that element, so a comma separates it from “hands.” The semicolon after “respectively” then joins the first independent clause to the second, “percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane.”

A.why_wrong: A comma after “respectively” can’t join the first independent clause to “percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane”; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark after “respectively,” the first independent clause runs straight into the second, “percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane,” so the two clauses are fused without punctuation.

D.why_wrong: The dash after “respectively” pairs with the dash after “dimensions” to close the supplementary element, so it can’t also mark the boundary between the two independent clauses; the clauses are left without a proper joining mark.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music: the tabla's narrow wooden right-hand treble drum and broader metal or clay left-hand bass drum); real subject, no person named. items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a complex series, with a second slot inside the first item
items.passage: Steelpans, the percussion instruments that Trinidadian musicians fashioned from discarded oil drums in the 1940s, are organized in a steel orchestra by ______ the tenor pans, which carry the melody; in the middle, the guitar and cello pans, which supply rhythmic chords; and at the bottom, the bass pans, each constructed from an entire drum.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Steelpans ... are organized in a steel orchestra by range” is a complete clause, and what follows is a list of the groups, separated by semicolons because each item contains commas. A colon after “range” introduces that list, and the comma after “at the top” separates the first item’s position from the pans it names, as the commas after “in the middle” and “at the bottom” do in the later items.

A.why_wrong: A comma can’t introduce a list whose items are separated by semicolons; after “range,” the list of groups needs a colon to set it up.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “at the top, the tenor pans, which carry the melody” is the first item of a list, not a clause.

D.why_wrong: With no colon, “at the top” runs into the clause (“organized in a steel orchestra by range at the top”), and nothing introduces the list of groups that follows.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music: steel orchestra sections, tenor, guitar and cello, and bass pans; pans made from oil drums in 1940s Trinidad); real subject, no person named. items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase whose relative clause and so-that clause hold finite verbs
items.passage: Most diamonds form more than 150 kilometers below Earth’s surface, far deeper than any mine has ever reached. The gems are carried upward by a rare and violent type of ______ kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma from the mantle through narrow pipes so quickly that the diamonds reach the surface before they can turn into graphite.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The gems are carried upward by a rare and violent type of volcanism” is a complete clause that announces something, and the noun phrase “kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma ... before they can turn into graphite” names that type of volcanism. A colon after “volcanism” introduces this explanation.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma from the mantle through narrow pipes so quickly that the diamonds reach the surface before they can turn into graphite” has no main verb (“drive” belongs to the which-clause and “reach” to the that-clause), so it isn’t a clause.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “type of volcanism kimberlite eruptions” runs the noun phrase into the clause, and nothing marks it as the explanation of what that type of volcanism is.

D.why_wrong: With a period, “Kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma from the mantle ... before they can turn into graphite” would stand alone as a sentence, but all of its verbs are inside the which-clause, so it is a fragment.
