items.subtype: No punctuation between a title and a name, or between the name and its verb
items.passage: Between the eighth and tenth centuries, visitors to Sigiriya, a rock fortress in Sri Lanka, inscribed hundreds of poems on a polished wall. In 1956, after years spent deciphering the faded, often overlapping lines, Sri Lankan ______ published translations of 685 of these verses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Senarath Paranavithana” identifies which Sri Lankan epigraphist is meant, so it is essential information and isn’t set off from the title “Sri Lankan epigraphist” with punctuation. No punctuation is needed after the name either, because “Sri Lankan epigraphist Senarath Paranavithana” is the subject of the verb “published.”

A.why_wrong: Commas around “Senarath Paranavithana” treat the name as extra information, but with no article before the title, the name is essential; it identifies the epigraphist, so it shouldn’t be set off.

B.why_wrong: The comma after “Paranavithana” separates the subject, “Sri Lankan epigraphist Senarath Paranavithana,” from its verb, “published.”

C.why_wrong: The comma after “epigraphist” separates the title from the essential name that identifies it, and it is left without a partner before the verb.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a title and a name
items.passage: Tengenenge, a stone sculpture community in northern Zimbabwe, was founded in 1966 by tobacco ______ Tom Blomefield, who, after international sanctions crippled his business, invited the workers on his farm to try carving the serpentine stone found there.

items.subtype: Closing comma of an appositive that contains its own comma-set appositive

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “Cheomseongdae, a bottle-shaped granite tower ... in the seventh century” has no verb of its own.

C.why_wrong: A dash can’t close a supplementary element that a comma opened after “Cheomseongdae”; the marks must match.

items.notes: Subject: history and science (Cheomseongdae, the Silla-period granite tower in Gyeongju from Queen Seondeok's reign, often called East Asia's oldest surviving observatory); real subject, standard facts. Band 6: the S3_comma_pair hard cell has only one official (3.12, band 6), and the comma-pair shape whose partner sits far back is 2.14's; here the partner is 22 words back and a second comma pair nested inside the element (“the capital of the Silla kingdom”) tempts a student to think the element already closed. Every wrong option fails on a rule.

band7.why: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items, so a strong band 6: the partner comma is 22 words back with a nested comma pair inside the element.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: From 1866 until 1984, a network of underground tubes connected post offices throughout Paris, carrying messages in canisters propelled by compressed air. Messages sent this way usually arrived within a few ______ Parisians came to rely on these “petits bleus,” named for their blue paper, for urgent notes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Messages sent this way usually arrived within a few hours” is an independent clause, and so is the clause that follows, which begins “Parisians came to rely on these” and ends “for urgent notes.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When “and” joins two independent clauses of this length, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two independent clauses; without a conjunction, the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Paris pneumatic post, 1866 to 1984, its blue message forms called petits bleus); real subject, no person named. Medium: the standard 8-of-11 menu (and / , and / , / none); no semicolon or period option (a twin of the key).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence opens with a short prepositional phrase
items.passage: Pearlfish, slender, eel-like fish that shelter inside living sea cucumbers after entering tail first through an opening at the host’s rear, typically leave their hosts at night to hunt small ______ a few species, the fish remain permanently inside and feed on the sea cucumber’s reproductive organs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Pearlfish ... typically leave their hosts at night to hunt small crustaceans” is a complete sentence. “In a few species” is an introductory phrase that begins the next sentence, whose subject and verb are “the fish remain.” A period after “crustaceans” marks the boundary between the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “in a few species” seems to belong to the first sentence, but “the fish remain permanently inside and feed on the sea cucumber’s reproductive organs” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, “and” can’t join these two independent clauses (“Pearlfish ... typically leave their hosts” and “the fish remain permanently inside”).

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “small crustaceans in a few species” runs the introductory phrase into the first sentence, and the independent clause “the fish remain permanently inside” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: science (pearlfish, Carapidae, sheltering in sea cucumbers; most hunt small crustaceans at night, a few species live permanently inside and eat the host's gonads); real subject, no researcher named. Medium: a 4-word prepositional opener (2.7, 2.9 type), menu of 2.7 and 2.27 (period / comma / none / and). No semicolon option (twin) and no “, and” option (legal).

items.subtype: Closing comma of an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: Each pyrosome, a hollow tube made up of thousands of genetically identical animals known as ______ drifts through warm seas worldwide, propelled by a gentle jet that its members create by pumping seawater through the colony’s wall.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “pyrosome” opens a supplementary element, “a hollow tube made up of thousands of genetically identical animals known as zooids,” that describes the pyrosome. A comma after “zooids” closes that element, pairing with the first comma, so the main clause reads “Each pyrosome ... drifts through warm seas worldwide.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma after “zooids,” the supplementary element opened by the comma after “pyrosome” is never closed.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “Each pyrosome, a hollow tube made up of thousands of genetically identical animals known as zooids” has no main verb.

D.why_wrong: A dash can’t close a supplementary element that a comma opened; the marks around the description of the pyrosome must match.

items.notes: Subject: science (pyrosomes, colonial tunicates made of budded, genetically identical zooids that pump water to move the colony); real subject, no researcher named. Medium: 2.1 shape and menu (comma / none / semicolon / dash); the partner comma is 13 words back.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: At the hydrothermal field of Dallol, which lies below sea level in Ethiopia’s Danakil Depression, one of the hottest regions on Earth, scalding, acidic water percolates up through thick salt deposits and pools at the ______ the ground in vivid shades of yellow, green, and orange as dissolved minerals crystallize.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “scalding, acidic water percolates up through thick salt deposits and pools at the surface” is the main clause, and “staining the ground in vivid shades of yellow, green, and orange as dissolved minerals crystallize” is a participial phrase that describes what the water does as it collects. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this supplementary phrase.

A.why_wrong: With a period, “Staining the ground in vivid shades of yellow, green, and orange as dissolved minerals crystallize” would stand alone as a sentence, but it has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the participial phrase beginning “staining the ground” isn’t a clause.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the participial phrase runs into the main clause and seems to describe “the surface” rather than the water; a comma is needed before this supplementary phrase.

items.notes: Subject: science (the Dallol hydrothermal field in Ethiopia's Danakil Depression, below sea level, hot acidic brine, yellow, green and orange mineral deposits); real subject, no figures, no person named. Medium: 2.4 and 2.26 menu (period / comma / semicolon / none) with an -ing tail after a long one-sentence run.

items.subtype: Closing dash of a dash pair between subject and verb
items.passage: Rosemaling—a style of decorative painting that flourished in the rural valleys of Norway from about 1750 to ______ covered wooden chests, bowls, and walls with swirling scrolls and stylized flowers, and Norwegian immigrants later brought it to the United States.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “Rosemaling” opens a supplementary element that defines the term, “a style of decorative painting that flourished in the rural valleys of Norway from about 1750 to 1850.” A dash after “1850” closes that element, pairing with the first dash, so the main clause reads “Rosemaling ... covered wooden chests, bowls, and walls with swirling scrolls and stylized flowers.”

A.why_wrong: A comma can’t close a supplementary element that a dash opened; the marks around the definition of rosemaling must match.

B.why_wrong: Without a mark after “1850,” the supplementary element opened by the dash after “Rosemaling” is never closed.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the words before the blank (“Rosemaling” and the definition after it) have no main verb, so they aren’t a clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts (rosemaling, Norwegian decorative folk painting of about 1750 to 1850 on chests, bowls and walls, carried to the United States by immigrants); real subject, no person named. Medium: 2.13 menu (semicolon / none / comma / dash) with the partner dash 17 words back.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause: semicolon before “however,” comma after
items.passage: After their expulsion from Spain in 1492, many Sephardic Jews settled in the Ottoman Empire, where their Spanish evolved into Ladino. For centuries, Ladino thrived in cities such as Salonica, supporting newspapers and a rich tradition of ______ the language declined sharply in the twentieth century as communities were destroyed or dispersed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “For centuries, Ladino thrived in cities such as Salonica, supporting newspapers and a rich tradition of ballads” and “the language declined sharply in the twentieth century as communities were destroyed or dispersed” are both independent clauses, so a semicolon after “ballads” joins them. The adverb “however” begins the second clause, which contrasts with the first, and is followed by a comma.

B.why_wrong: Commas around “however” can’t join two independent clauses; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark before “however,” the adverb runs into the first clause, and the two independent clauses are then joined by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together: “a rich tradition of ballads the language declined sharply.”

items.notes: Subject: language (Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish of Sephardic Jews in Ottoman cities such as Salonica, with its newspapers and ballads, and its twentieth-century decline); real subject, no person named. Replaced a Baybayin draft that repeated item 01's early-Philippine-writing theme. Medium: 2.8 shape (adverb opens clause 2) with the a9e5b788 drop-the-adverb option; every option that has “however” puts a comma after it, so it can’t read as “in whatever way”; no “, however;” option (it would fail only on meaning) and no period option (twin).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Flying fish inhabit tropical and subtropical oceans around the world. To escape predators such as tuna, they leap out of the water and glide ______ the waves on stiff, winglike fins, sometimes traveling more than 50 meters in a single flight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: No punctuation is needed between the preposition “over” and its object, “the waves.” Together they tell where the fish glide.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “To escape predators such as tuna, they leap out of the water and glide over” is incomplete; the preposition needs its object.

B.why_wrong: A comma shouldn’t separate the preposition “over” from its object, “the waves.”

C.why_wrong: A dash shouldn’t come between the preposition and its object, and nothing else in the sentence pairs with it.

items.notes: Subject: science (flying fish: leaping from the water and gliding on enlarged, winglike fins to escape predators, glides of 50 meters or more); standard natural history, no researcher named. Replaced in review: the draft's subject (sand cats) is an official Text Structure and Purpose item (190857f0). Easy: preposition plus object, menu of colon, comma, dash and none (1.5, 1.9).

fixes: new subject (flying fish): the draft's sand cat is official Text Structure and Purpose item 190857f0; same preposition-object build, menu and key letter

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Launched by the government of the Indian state of Kerala in 1998, Kudumbashree organizes women into small neighborhood groups. Members pool their savings, lend money to one another, and ______ small businesses such as tailoring shops, farms, and cafés.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The verb “start” and its object, “small businesses,” form the last of the three actions listed for the members, so no punctuation should come between them.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “Members pool their savings, lend money to one another, and start” is incomplete; the verb needs its object.

B.why_wrong: A dash shouldn’t separate the verb “start” from its object, “small businesses,” and nothing else in the sentence pairs with it.

D.why_wrong: A comma between “start” and “small businesses” splits the verb from its object; no punctuation belongs there.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Kudumbashree, Kerala's women's neighborhood-group network launched by the state government in 1998: savings, loans, small enterprises); real subject, no person named. Easy: verb plus object inside a three-part series of verb phrases; the blank is after the verb of item 3, not at a series comma.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: In Basque bertsolaritza, singers improvise verses on topics given to them moments earlier. The verses must follow strict rules of rhyme and ______ skilled singers compose them almost instantly, often before large crowds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The verses must follow strict rules of rhyme and meter” and “skilled singers compose them almost instantly” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and marks the contrast between the strict rules and the singers’ speed.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two independent clauses; the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: literature (bertsolaritza, Basque improvised sung verse on topics set just before performing, with strict rhyme and meter); real subject, no person named. Easy: the 1.2 and 1.27 menu (, but / but / , / none). The “and” before the blank is inside clause 1 (“rhyme and meter”), not a joining word.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Although the fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded is not known to have written anything ______ vakhs, or short mystical verses, have survived for more than six centuries, preserved by devotees who memorized and recited them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Although the fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded is not known to have written anything down” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause, whose subject and verb are “her vakhs ... have survived.” A comma after “down” separates the introductory clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the clause beginning “Although” is dependent, so it can’t stand on one side of a semicolon.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs into the main clause (“written anything down her vakhs”); a comma is needed after an introductory clause like this one.

D.why_wrong: With a period, “Although the fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded is not known to have written anything down” would stand alone as a sentence, but it is a dependent clause, so it is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Lal Ded, or Lalleshwari, fourteenth-century Kashmiri mystic poet whose vakhs survived through oral recitation); real subject. Easy: Although-clause (1.8) with the menu semicolon / comma / none / period.

items.subtype: Indirect question inside a statement: statement word order and a period
items.passage: At Lothal, an Indus Valley city in western India, archaeologists uncovered a large rectangular basin lined with fired bricks. Some believe boats docked there, while others argue that it functioned as a reservoir; scholars still debate what purpose ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The last clause is a statement about what scholars debate, and “what purpose the basin served” is an indirect question within it. An indirect question takes statement word order, with the subject “the basin” before the verb “served,” and the sentence ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: This choice uses the word order and question mark of a direct question, but the sentence is a statement about what scholars debate, so the indirect question needs statement order and a period.

B.why_wrong: The word order is right for an indirect question, but the sentence as a whole is a statement, so it should end with a period, not a question mark.

C.why_wrong: The inverted word order (“did the basin serve”) belongs to a direct question; inside a statement, the indirect question needs statement order: “the basin served.”

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (the brick basin at Lothal, read as a dockyard by some and a reservoir by others); real debate, no person named. Easy: the 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark (1.7, 1.24), with the blank ending the passage as in 1.24.

review.note: Shares the Indus civilization with official Inferences item 4e9afd7a but not its subject (the Lothal basin debate); acceptable.

items.subtype: Comma between items of a simple series (blank after item 1)
items.passage: Hong Kong’s Octopus card, introduced in 1997, was among the first contactless payment cards in widespread use. Commuters first used it to pay train and bus fares, but today it also pays for groceries at convenience ______ snacks from vending machines, and parking at meters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things the card pays for: “groceries at convenience stores,” “snacks from vending machines,” and “parking at meters.” A comma after “stores” separates the first item from the second, just as the comma after “machines” separates the second from the third.

A.why_wrong: Semicolons separate the items in a list only when the items themselves contain commas; these items don’t, so a comma is needed.

C.why_wrong: A colon can’t be used between two items in a list; “snacks from vending machines” is the second item, not an explanation of the first.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the first and second items run together (“convenience stores snacks”).

items.notes: Subject: social science (Hong Kong's Octopus card, 1997, an early contactless payment card later used beyond transit); real subject. Easy: simple series with the blank after item 1, as in 1.3, 1.12 and 1.25, never at the optional serial-comma slot.

items.subtype: No punctuation before a restrictive that-clause (relative pronoun needed)
items.passage: For years, home internet access in Cuba was rare and costly. Many Cubans instead relied on el paquete semanal (“the weekly package”), a bundle of digital ______ travels from home to home each week on portable hard drives, bringing films, TV shows, music, and magazines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “that travels from home to home each week on portable hard drives” tells which bundle of digital files is meant, so it is essential and isn’t set off with punctuation. The relative pronoun “that” is needed as the clause’s subject; without it, the verb “travels” has nothing to attach to.

A.why_wrong: A dash shouldn’t separate “files” from the essential clause beginning “that travels,” and nothing else in the sentence pairs with it.

B.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb “travels” has no subject of its own, so “a bundle of digital files travels from home to home” can’t fit into the sentence.

D.why_wrong: A comma shouldn’t come before “that” here: the clause it begins is essential to the meaning of “a bundle of digital files,” and essential relative clauses aren’t set off with a comma.

items.notes: Subject: social science (el paquete semanal, Cuba's weekly offline media collection carried on hard drives); real subject, no person named. Easy: 1.29 shape (the relative pronoun is the clause's subject, so the no-that option is ungrammatical) with a stray-dash option in place of 1.29's bare comma.
